title: Establish AI Data Governance, Lineage, and Accountability
intro: Who is accountable for AI data (owners, stewards, custodians, controllers and processors); sovereignty, residency and cross-border transfers; classification, tagging and sensitive data impact assessments; provenance, lineage and sourcing of real and synthetic data; chain-of-custody controls; and the AI data lifecycle from collection to deletion.
objectives: Assign data ownership roles for AI data, and apply controller and processor roles to AI providers
Distinguish data sovereignty, residency and localisation, and control cross-border AI processing
Design classification schemes with AI handling rules, tagging that survives AI pipelines, and sensitive data impact assessments
Record provenance and lineage for real and synthetic data, and apply chain-of-custody controls
Apply controls at each stage of the AI data lifecycle, and propagate deletion downstream

sections.title: Data ownership roles, sovereignty and residency

blocks.title: Who owns the data, and where may it go?

scenes.title: Who owns the data, and where may it go?
scenes.sub: Ownership roles, controllers and processors, sovereignty and residency
scenes.say: Every dataset that feeds an AI system needs someone accountable for it, and a clear answer to where it may be stored and processed. | This video covers the data ownership roles you must know, how controller and processor roles apply to AI, and the difference between sovereignty, residency and localisation.

scenes.title: Data roles

items.d: Accountable: sets classification, approves access and use
Day-to-day quality, metadata and standards
Operates storage, backups and technical controls
Decides the purposes and means of processing
Processes personal data on the controller’s behalf
The person the data is about

scenes.say: Six roles appear again and again. | The information owner, or data owner, is accountable for a dataset. They decide its classification and approve who may access it and for what. | The data steward looks after it day to day: quality, metadata and standards. | The data custodian operates the storage, backups and technical controls, usually in IT or a platform team. | Under privacy law, the controller decides the purposes and means of processing personal data. | The processor processes personal data on the controller’s behalf, following its instructions. | And the data subject is the person the data is about.

scenes.title: Controller or processor in AI?
rows: Yes: why and how data is processed
A bank running an AI complaints assistant
A model provider that doesn’t use the data for itself
scenes.say: Controller and processor roles apply to AI just as to any other processing. | The controller decides why and how personal data is processed. The processor acts only on the controller’s documented instructions. | The controller carries the main duties: lawful basis, impact assessments, individuals’ rights and transparency. The processor must keep data secure and confidential, assist the controller, and notify it of breaches. | A bank running an AI complaints assistant is the controller. A model provider that processes prompts only to serve the bank is its processor. But if the provider also uses those prompts to train its own models, it is deciding a purpose of its own, and becomes a controller for that processing.

scenes.title: Ownership questions AI raises

items.d: Who owns, and may approve, each source?
Who owns embeddings, features and labels?
Who owns, checks and retains what the model produces?
Who approves reusing data for a new AI purpose?

scenes.say: AI raises ownership questions that traditional governance often leaves open. | Training data: who owns each source, and who may approve its use for training? | Derived data: who owns the embeddings, features and labels created from source data? They usually inherit the source’s classification and owner. | Outputs: who owns, checks and retains what the model produces? | And new uses: who approves reusing existing data for a new AI purpose? Purpose changes are where many privacy breaches begin.

scenes.title: Sovereignty, residency and localisation

layers.label: Data sovereignty
layers.sub: Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is located or controlled

layers.label: Data residency
layers.sub: Where data is stored and processed: a policy or contractual choice

layers.label: Data localisation
layers.sub: A legal requirement that data stays within a country’s borders

scenes.say: Three terms are easily confused. | Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it is located, or of the country whose authorities can compel access to it. | Data residency is where data is physically stored and processed. It is usually a business, policy or contractual choice. | And data localisation is a legal requirement that certain data must stay within a country’s borders. Residency choices are often made to satisfy sovereignty concerns and localisation laws.

scenes.title: Cross-border questions for AI

items.d: Prompts may be processed in another region
Datasets move to wherever the compute is
Models trained on regulated data may need to stay put
Support staff abroad can count as a transfer
Each may add another country
Adequacy, contractual clauses or binding rules

scenes.say: AI creates new cross-border questions. | Where does inference happen? Some services route prompts to whichever region has capacity. | Where does training happen? Datasets tend to move to wherever the compute is. | Where are the model weights? A model trained on regulated data may itself need to stay within certain borders. | Who has remote access? Support or engineering staff in another country can count as a transfer. | Which sub-processors are involved? Each can add another country. | And which legal mechanism covers any transfer of personal data, such as an adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules?

items: Owner accountable; steward manages; custodian operates
Controller decides purpose; processor follows instructions
Using customer data for your own training makes you a controller
Sovereignty is legal reach; residency is location; localisation is a mandate
scenes.say: To recap. | The data owner is accountable, the steward manages day to day, and the custodian operates the technical controls. | The controller decides purposes and means; the processor follows instructions. | A provider that uses customer data to train its own models becomes a controller for that purpose. | And sovereignty is about legal reach, residency about location, and localisation about legal mandates to keep data in-country.

blocks.md:
### Data ownership roles
| Role | Responsibilities | In AI programmes |
|---|---|---|
| **Information owner (data owner)** | Accountable for a dataset: classification, permitted uses, access approval, retention | Approves use of data for training, fine-tuning, evaluation and retrieval; accountable for derived data |
| **Data steward** | Day-to-day management: quality, definitions, metadata, standards | Maintains datasheets, quality checks, lineage metadata and labels |
| **Data custodian** | Technical operation: storage, backups, encryption, access enforcement | Operates data lakes, feature stores, vector databases and training data stores |
| **Data controller** (GDPR) | Determines purposes and means of processing personal data | The organisation deploying the AI system, or any party using data for its own purposes |
| **Data processor** (GDPR) | Processes personal data on behalf of, and on the instructions of, a controller | Model API providers, annotation vendors, hosting providers acting only on instructions |
| **Joint controllers** | Two or more parties jointly determine purposes and means | Partners co-developing a model on pooled data |
| **Data subject** | The identified or identifiable person | Customers, employees, patients and members of the public in datasets |

Two principles keep this workable:
- **Every dataset, derived dataset and model has a named owner.** Derived artefacts such as embeddings, features, labels and synthetic data usually inherit the classification and ownership of their source unless the owner decides otherwise.
- **Purpose changes need the owner’s approval** (and often a fresh privacy assessment). Reusing customer service transcripts to train a model is a new purpose, even if the data never leaves the organisation.

### Controllers and processors in AI
A provider is a **processor** when it processes personal data only to deliver the service on the customer’s documented instructions. If it uses customer data for its own purposes, such as **training or improving its models**, it acts as a **controller** for that processing and needs its own lawful basis. This is why enterprise AI contracts commit providers not to train on customer data, and why the role analysis must be documented in the **data processing agreement** (GDPR Article 28), which must cover subject matter, duration, purpose, data types, security measures, sub-processors and assistance with rights and breaches.

### Sovereignty, residency and localisation
- **Data sovereignty:** data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it resides and, for some laws, of the jurisdiction of the company that controls it, wherever it is stored. Concerns about foreign government access drive demand for **sovereign cloud** and **sovereign AI** offerings, where data, models and operations stay under local control.
- **Data residency:** the geographic location where data is stored and processed, chosen to meet legal, contractual or customer requirements.
- **Data localisation:** laws requiring certain data, such as health, financial, government or “important” data, to stay within national borders, or restricting its export.

### Cross-border transfers and AI
Under the GDPR (Chapter V), personal data may leave the European Economic Area only with a valid mechanism: an **adequacy decision** (such as the EU–US Data Privacy Framework for certified US companies), **standard contractual clauses** or **binding corporate rules**, supported by transfer impact assessments where needed. Other countries have their own export rules. For AI, map and control:
1. **Inference location:** where prompts and outputs are processed, including failover regions and “global” routing options.
2. **Training and fine-tuning location:** where datasets are copied for training runs.
3. **Model location:** where weights trained on regulated data are stored and served.
4. **Logging and monitoring location:** abuse-monitoring logs and telemetry may be stored elsewhere.
5. **Human access:** remote support or annotation staff in other countries.
6. **Sub-processors:** each adds locations and legal exposure.

Most major AI providers now offer regional processing and data-residency options; selecting and contractually locking them is a governance decision for the data owner, not a default to assume.

blocks.title: Name the role
pairs: Decides that customer emails may be used to fine-tune a support model
Maintains the dataset’s datasheet and quality checks
Runs the vector database backups and encryption
A model API provider serving prompts only on the customer’s instructions
The same provider using customer prompts to train its next model

blocks.title: Accountability vs operation
blocks.md: The **owner** is accountable and makes decisions (classification, access, use). The **custodian** implements and operates controls on the owner’s behalf. If a question asks who should approve using a dataset for model training, the answer is the **data owner**, not the custodian, the data scientist or the security team.

q.q: A company’s AI provider processes prompts in its EU region by default but fails over to US data centres during peak demand. The company has committed to EU-only processing for a public-sector client. What is the BEST action?
o: Accept the failover, since it happens rarely and the provider’s data centres meet the same security standards
Contractually lock processing to EU regions with no cross-region failover, verify it, and confirm sub-processors
Ask users to avoid peak times, and monitor how often failover to the US data centres actually occurs
Encrypt all prompts in transit and at rest, so that data processed in the US remains protected from any access
q.why: Residency commitments must hold in all conditions, including failover. Contractual and technical locking, verified configuration and sub-processor review deliver them. Encryption in transit doesn’t change where data is processed.

sections.title: Data classification, tagging and sensitive data impact assessments

blocks.title: Label it before you learn from it

scenes.title: Label it before you learn from it
scenes.sub: Classification, tagging, and assessing sensitive data for AI
scenes.say: An AI pipeline can’t protect data it can’t recognise. Classification and tagging are how data tells every downstream system how it must be handled. | This video covers classification schemes, tagging that survives AI pipelines, how labels drive AI controls, and the sensitive data impact assessment.

scenes.title: A classification scheme for AI (example)

layers.label: Restricted
layers.sub: Special category, cardholder, secrets: isolated approved systems only

layers.label: Confidential
layers.sub: Customer data, contracts, code: enterprise AI with no-training terms

layers.label: Internal
layers.sub: Policies, internal reports: approved AI tools

layers.label: Public
layers.sub: Published material: any tool, still check outputs

scenes.say: Most organisations use three to five classification levels. Here is an example with AI handling rules attached. | Restricted data, such as special category data, cardholder data and secrets, never goes to external AI, only to approved, isolated systems. | Confidential data, such as customer records, contracts and source code, may only go to approved enterprise AI services with no-training commitments. | Internal data, such as policies and internal reports, may be used with approved AI tools. | And public data can go into any tool, though outputs still need checking.

scenes.title: Tagging that survives AI pipelines

items.d: The owner knows the data best; tools make it easy
Pattern matching and ML classifiers find what was missed
Carried into chunks, embeddings and datasets
Consent, permitted uses, residency, licence, retention

scenes.say: Tagging has to survive the journey through AI pipelines. | Owners apply labels, because they know the data best, and tools should make labelling easy. | Automated discovery, using pattern matching and machine learning classifiers, finds sensitive data that nobody labelled. | Labels must travel as metadata: when a document is split into chunks and embedded, each chunk must keep its label. | And AI needs extra attributes beyond sensitivity: consent status, permitted uses, residency, licence and retention.

scenes.title: Labels driving AI controls
scenes.say: Here is how labels drive controls in a retrieval system. A document arrives labelled confidential. | An ingestion gate checks whether that label is allowed in this index. A restricted document would be rejected. | In the index, every chunk and embedding keeps the label. | At retrieval, results are filtered by the user’s clearance, so nobody receives content above their level. | The generated answer inherits the highest label of the content it used. | And data loss prevention at egress blocks the answer from going anywhere the label forbids, such as an external email.

scenes.title: Sensitive data impact assessment

items.d: New sensitive dataset for AI, or a new use of one
Categories, volume, subjects, sensitivity
Is the AI use compatible with why it was collected?
Inference, memorisation, re-identification
Minimise, de-identify, isolate, restrict access
Approve, approve with conditions, or refuse

scenes.say: Before sensitive data is used for AI, a sensitive data impact assessment examines it. | It is triggered by a new sensitive dataset entering an AI pipeline, or a new use of an existing one. | It profiles the data: categories, volume, whose data it is, and how sensitive. | It tests purpose fit: is the AI use compatible with the purpose the data was collected for? | It considers derivation risks: inference of new sensitive facts, memorisation and re-identification. | It specifies safeguards: minimisation, de-identification, isolation and access restrictions. | And it ends with a decision: approve, approve with conditions, or refuse. It often feeds a DPIA.

scenes.title: Classification pitfalls in AI

items.d: Chunking, embedding and joins drop metadata
Harmless pieces combine into sensitive wholes
Generated summaries of confidential data
If everything is secret, labels get ignored

scenes.say: Watch for four pitfalls. | Labels lost in transformation: chunking, embedding and joining datasets often drop metadata unless pipelines carry it deliberately. | Aggregation raises sensitivity: individually harmless records can combine into something sensitive, sometimes called the mosaic effect. | Unlabelled AI output: a summary of a confidential report is still confidential, but it rarely carries a label. | And over-classification: if everything is marked secret, people stop paying attention to labels at all.

items: Attach AI handling rules to each classification level
Tags must survive chunking and embedding
Labels drive ingestion, retrieval filtering and DLP
Assess sensitive data before AI use: purpose, derivation, safeguards
scenes.say: To recap. | Attach clear AI handling rules to each classification level. | Make sure tags survive chunking, embedding and every other transformation. | Use labels to drive ingestion gates, retrieval filtering and data loss prevention. | And run a sensitive data impact assessment before sensitive data is used for AI, covering purpose fit, derivation risks and safeguards.

blocks.md:
### Classification for AI
**Data classification** assigns a sensitivity level to data based on the impact of its unauthorised disclosure, modification or loss. Typical schemes use three to five levels (for example, Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted). For AI, each level needs explicit handling rules:

| Level | Examples | AI handling (example) |
|---|---|---|
| **Restricted** | Special category data, cardholder data, credentials and keys, M&A plans, export-controlled data | Not permitted in external AI services; only approved, isolated environments with additional controls; SDIA required |
| **Confidential** | Customer and employee personal data, contracts, source code, unreleased financials | Approved enterprise AI with no-training and retention terms; retrieval with permission filtering |
| **Internal** | Policies, internal communications, general business documents | Approved AI tools |
| **Public** | Published content | Any tool; verify outputs before reuse |

The classification is set by the **data owner**, informed by legal and regulatory requirements. **Declassification** and **reclassification** rules matter too: an aggregated or de-identified dataset may move down a level, and an enriched or combined one may move up.

### Tagging and labelling
- **Manual labelling** by owners or authors, supported by sensible defaults (for example, a team site defaulting to Confidential).
- **Automated classification** using pattern matching (card numbers, national IDs), exact data matching against known records, and ML classifiers for documents such as contracts or medical notes. **Data security posture management (DSPM)** tools (Module 3.4) discover and classify data across cloud stores, including AI training buckets and vector databases.
- **Label persistence:** pipelines must propagate labels from source documents to **chunks, embeddings, features, datasets and outputs**. Vector databases should store labels and access-control metadata with each chunk so retrieval can filter on them.
- **AI-specific attributes:** consent status, lawful basis, **permitted purposes** (for example, “may be used for retrieval but not for training”), residency constraints, licence terms, retention period and provenance.

### Labels as enforcement
Labels are only useful if systems act on them:
- **Ingestion gates** reject or route data whose label isn’t permitted for a given pipeline or index.
- **Retrieval filters** return only content the requesting user (or agent, acting for a user) is cleared to see.
- **Output labelling** marks generated content with the highest classification of its inputs.
- **DLP** enforces handling rules at egress points such as email, file sharing and external AI tools.
- **Agent data access** is constrained by labels and purposes (Module 3.4 covers purpose-based access and agentic data catalogues).

### Sensitive data impact assessment (SDIA)
An **SDIA** is a focused assessment carried out before sensitive or restricted data is used in an AI system (or used for a new purpose). It typically covers:
1. **Data profile:** categories (personal, special category, financial, health, children’s), volume, data subjects, sources, classification.
2. **Purpose and compatibility:** the intended AI use and whether it is compatible with the original collection purpose and legal basis.
3. **Access:** who and what (people, services, agents, vendors) will access the data, and where.
4. **Derivation risks:** attribute inference, memorisation and extraction, embedding inversion, re-identification through linkage.
5. **Safeguards:** minimisation, de-identification (Module 3.2), segregation, encryption, access control, output filtering, retention limits.
6. **Residual risk and decision:** approve, approve with conditions, or refuse; with owner sign-off and review triggers.

An SDIA frequently provides the data-specific input to a DPIA (Module 2.3), and its conditions become requirements for the pipeline.

### Pitfalls
- Labels dropped during chunking, embedding, feature engineering or joins.
- **Aggregation (mosaic) risk:** combining datasets can create data more sensitive than any part.
- AI-generated summaries, translations and extracts of sensitive content left unlabelled.
- **Over-classification**, which leads to label fatigue and workarounds; and **under-classification** of legacy data that was never assessed.

blocks.title: Classifying AI artefacts
items: Embeddings
Inherit the classification of their source text, because they can be partly inverted and are used to retrieve the source. A vector index built from Confidential documents is Confidential.
Fine-tuned models
May memorise training data. A model fine-tuned on Restricted data should be treated as Restricted unless testing shows otherwise and the owner approves reclassification.
Synthetic datasets
Classify according to their residual risk: high-fidelity synthetic data can leak real records. Validate privacy before lowering the classification.
Prompts and logs
Take the highest classification of content users may enter. Logs of a legal assistant’s prompts are as sensitive as the legal documents themselves.
Generated outputs
Inherit the highest label of their inputs, and may need a higher label if they aggregate sensitive facts.

blocks.title: Derived data inherits
blocks.md: A recurring exam theme: **derived artefacts inherit the classification of their sources** unless the owner, after assessment, decides otherwise. Embeddings, fine-tuned models, prompt logs and summaries of confidential data are not automatically less sensitive than the data they came from.

q.q: A team builds a vector index from Confidential HR documents and plans to classify the index as Internal because “it only contains numbers”. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, since embeddings are numerical vectors that can’t be read or linked to employees
Classify the index as Confidential, label each chunk with access metadata, and filter retrieval by clearance
Classify the index as Internal, but restrict the vector database to the HR team’s own isolated network segment
Delete the source documents after indexing, so only the less sensitive embeddings remain stored
q.why: Embeddings can be partly inverted and are used to retrieve the original text, so they inherit the source classification. Labels and access metadata per chunk enable permission-aware retrieval.

sections.title: Provenance, lineage, sourcing and chain of custody

blocks.title: Where did this data come from?

scenes.title: Where did this data come from?
scenes.sub: Provenance, lineage, real and synthetic sources, and chain of custody
scenes.say: When a model misbehaves, investigators ask where its data came from, who touched it, and what changed along the way. Without good records, those questions have no answers. | This video covers provenance, lineage and chain of custody, and how to source real and synthetic data responsibly.

scenes.title: Three related records
rows: How did it flow and change?
Who held it, and was it altered?
scenes.say: Three kinds of record work together. | Provenance answers: where did this data originate? Lineage answers: how did it flow and change on its way into a model? Chain of custody answers: who held it at each step, and can we prove it wasn’t altered? | Provenance focuses on source, collection method, licence and consent. Lineage focuses on transformations, dataset versions and the models trained on them. Chain of custody focuses on hand-offs, access and integrity. | Provenance supports decisions about rights and trust. Lineage supports impact analysis and reproducibility. And chain of custody provides evidence, for investigations, audits and disputes.

scenes.title: Real and synthetic data
rows: Faithful to reality, including its quirks
Privacy, scale, rare and edge cases
Fidelity gaps, bias amplification, leaked real records
Generator, version, seed data, validation results
scenes.say: Data sources are increasingly a mix of real and synthetic. | Real data comes from actual events, people and systems. Synthetic data is generated by models or simulations. | Real data is faithful to reality, including its messy edge cases. Synthetic data can protect privacy, scale up quickly, and cover rare cases. | But real data brings privacy, bias, licensing and poisoning risks, while synthetic data can miss important patterns, amplify the biases of its generator, and even reproduce real records the generator memorised. | So provenance must record different things: collection method, consent and licence for real data; and the generator model, its version, the seed data and validation results for synthetic data.

scenes.title: A lineage record

note.text: Every arrow is recorded, so any model traces back to its sources.

scenes.say: Here is a lineage record end to end. It begins with sources, each with an owner, a licence and a consent status. | At ingestion, data is hashed, labelled and timestamped. | Transformation steps, such as cleaning, de-duplication and de-identification, are recorded with the code that performed them. | The result is a versioned, hashed dataset. | A training run records the dataset version, the code commit and the configuration. | And it produces a model version with its own hash and model card. Because every arrow is recorded, any model can be traced back to its sources, and any source forward to every model it touched.

scenes.title: Chain-of-custody controls

items.d: Detect any change between steps
Digital signatures prove origin and integrity
Tamper-evident records of access and transfer
Least privilege and approvals for each custodian
Check hashes and signatures before use

scenes.say: Chain of custody needs five controls. | Hash data at every hand-off, so any change between steps is detectable. | Digitally sign datasets and models you release, proving who produced them and that they are unaltered. | Keep append-only, tamper-evident logs of access and transfers. | Control access, with least privilege and approvals for each custodian, including vendors such as annotation companies. | And verify hashes and signatures on receipt, before anything is used for training or deployment.

items: Provenance: origin; lineage: flow; custody: who held it, unaltered
Real and synthetic data need different provenance records
Lineage links sources, versions, runs and models
Hash, sign, log, control access, verify on receipt
scenes.say: To recap. | Provenance records origin, lineage records flow and transformation, and chain of custody proves who held data and that it wasn’t altered. | Real and synthetic data need different provenance records. | Lineage links sources, dataset versions, training runs and models, in both directions. | And chain of custody relies on hashing, signing, append-only logs, controlled access and verification on receipt.

blocks.md:
### Provenance, lineage and chain of custody
| Record | Definition | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| **Provenance** | The origin and history of data | Source system or supplier, collection method and date, legal basis or consent, licence, original classification, known limitations |
| **Lineage** | The end-to-end flow of data through systems and transformations into downstream artefacts | Pipeline steps and code versions, dataset versions, joins, filters, de-identification steps, training runs, model versions, deployments |
| **Chain of custody** | A documented, tamper-evident record of who possessed, accessed or transferred data and when | Custodians, transfers, access events, integrity checks (hashes, signatures), approvals |

Together they let you answer: *Can we lawfully use this data? Which models did this record influence? Has anything been tampered with? Who is accountable at each step?* These questions arise in poisoning investigations, erasure requests, licence disputes, audits and regulatory inquiries. The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to apply data governance practices covering **data collection processes and the origin of data** (Article 10), and to keep technical documentation and logs that make traceability possible.

### Sourcing real and synthetic data
**Real data** should be sourced with due diligence: reputable suppliers, documented collection methods, lawful basis and consent, licence terms that permit AI use, and representativeness for the intended population. Avoid data of unknown provenance; if it can’t be traced, it can’t be trusted, defended or deleted on request.

**Synthetic data** is increasingly used to fill gaps, protect privacy and test systems. Its trustworthiness depends on:
- **Fidelity:** does it preserve the statistical properties and edge cases that matter for the task?
- **Privacy:** does it leak real records? Generators can memorise their seed data, so test for near-duplicates and membership inference before treating it as non-personal.
- **Bias:** generators reproduce, and can amplify, the biases of their training data.
- **Provenance:** record the generator model and version, prompts or parameters, seed data and its provenance, and validation results, and **label synthetic records as synthetic** so they can be excluded from future training where needed (avoiding the model collapse loop from Module 1.3).

### Lineage in practice
Lineage is captured automatically where possible: data catalogues and pipeline orchestrators record dataset versions, transformations and dependencies; ML platforms and model registries record training runs (dataset version, code commit, hyperparameters, environment) and resulting model versions. **Data versioning** tools give each dataset snapshot an immutable identifier (often a content hash), so a model can always be linked to the exact data it saw. Lineage should also extend to **retrieval indexes**, recording which source documents produced which chunks, so deletions and corrections propagate.

### Chain-of-custody controls
- **Cryptographic hashing** of datasets and files at ingestion and at every hand-off; mismatches indicate tampering or corruption.
- **Digital signatures** on datasets and models released between teams or to and from suppliers, proving origin and integrity (Module 3.6 covers model signing).
- **Append-only, tamper-evident logs** of access and transfers, protected from modification by the people whose actions they record.
- **Access control and approvals** for each custodian, including annotation vendors and contractors, with least privilege.
- **Verification on receipt** before data or models are used, and quarantine of anything that fails.
- **Retention of custody records** for as long as the data or models they describe remain in use, plus any legal requirement.

blocks.title: Provenance, lineage or chain of custody?
pairs: “This dataset was licensed from Supplier X under licence terms permitting model training.”
“Model v2.1 was trained on dataset v3, produced by pipeline commit a1b2c3.”
“The annotation vendor received the file at 09:14; its hash matched on return.”
“These records were generated by a simulator seeded with 2024 claims data.”

blocks.title: Traceability enables everything else
blocks.md: If a question asks what enables an organisation to determine **which models are affected** by a poisoned or unlawfully sourced dataset, the answer is **lineage** (supported by dataset versioning and AIBOMs). If it asks how to prove a dataset **wasn’t tampered with** between parties, the answer is **chain of custody** with hashes and signatures.

q.q: An annotation vendor returns a labelled dataset. What is the BEST way to confirm it wasn’t altered outside the agreed labelling changes?
o: Ask the vendor to confirm by email that only the agreed labelling changes were made to the data
Verify hashes and signatures against custody records, and compare returned data and label distributions
Train a model on the returned data and check that its accuracy matches previous training runs on the original
Rely on the vendor’s ISO 27001 certification, which covers the integrity of the data it processes
q.why: Chain-of-custody verification (hashes and signatures) detects unexpected changes to data, and statistical checks on labels catch unauthorised label modification. Assurances and downstream accuracy are weak substitutes.

scenes.title: The life of AI data
scenes.sub: Collection, validation, transformation, retention, archiving and deletion
scenes.say: Data for AI has a lifecycle, from the moment it is collected to the moment it is securely destroyed, and each stage needs its own controls. | This video walks through the AI data lifecycle, the controls at each stage, and why deletion has to travel all the way downstream.

scenes.title: The AI data lifecycle
scenes.intro: Each stage has an owner, controls and records.

stages.label: Use
stages.d: Training, retrieval, evaluation, under access control.

scenes.say: The AI data lifecycle has six stages. | Collection: data is gathered from lawful, documented sources, and only as much as the purpose needs. | Validation: it is checked for quality, schema, completeness and anomalies, including signs of poisoning. | Transformation: it is cleaned, labelled, de-identified and versioned, with every step recorded. | Use: it trains models, feeds retrieval systems and supports evaluation, under access control. | Retention and archiving: it is kept according to schedules and legal holds, in protected archives. | And deletion: it is securely destroyed when no longer needed, with deletion verified and propagated downstream.

scenes.title: Validation checks for AI data

items.d: Types, ranges, missing values
Compare with the expected baseline
Exact and near-duplicate records
Distribution shifts and noisy labels
Possible poisoning or corruption
Unexpected personal data or secrets

scenes.say: Validation is the first line of defence for data integrity. | Check schema and completeness: types, ranges and missing values. | Compare the statistical profile with an expected baseline, so unusual shifts stand out. | Find exact and near-duplicate records, which skew training and increase memorisation. | Check label quality: distributions that shift unexpectedly, or labels that disagree with the data. | Flag outliers and anomalies, which may signal poisoning or corruption. | And scan for unexpected sensitive content, such as personal data or secrets that shouldn’t be there.

scenes.title: Deletion must travel downstream
scenes.say: Deleting the source record is only the start. | Lineage tells you which dataset versions contain it, so they can be purged or flagged, and which retrieval indexes hold its chunks, so they can be deleted. | Models trained on it may need retraining or unlearning, according to a defined policy, and backups must expire on a known schedule. | And vendors that received the data must delete it too, and certify that they have. Without lineage, none of this can be scoped.

items: Collect, validate, transform, use, retain and archive, delete
Validation catches quality problems and poisoning early
Every transformation recorded and versioned
Deletion propagates through datasets, indexes, models, backups, vendors
scenes.say: To recap. | The AI data lifecycle runs from collection, validation and transformation, through use, to retention, archiving and deletion. | Validation catches quality problems and signs of poisoning early, before they reach a model. | Every transformation is recorded and versioned. | And deletion must propagate through dataset versions, indexes, models, backups and vendors.

blocks.md:
### Stage by stage
| Stage | Key controls | Records |
|---|---|---|
| **Collection** | Lawful basis and consent; minimisation; source vetting and licence checks; secure transfer; classification at ingestion | Provenance, datasheet, SDIA where sensitive |
| **Validation** | Schema and completeness checks; statistical profiling against baselines; duplicate detection; label quality checks; outlier and poisoning screening; sensitive-content scanning | Validation reports; quarantined items |
| **Transformation** | Documented, version-controlled code; reproducible pipelines; de-identification; labelling under quality control; augmentation and synthetic generation recorded | Lineage; dataset versions and hashes |
| **Use** (training, retrieval, evaluation) | Access control by purpose; segregation of regulated data; train/validation/test separation; encryption; monitoring of access | Training run records; access logs |
| **Retention and archiving** | Retention schedules per dataset and artefact; legal holds; protected, access-controlled archives; periodic review | Retention register; hold records |
| **Deletion** | Secure deletion and cryptographic erasure; propagation to derived artefacts, models, indexes, backups and vendors; verification | Deletion certificates and logs |

### Validation as a security control
Data validation is often thought of as a quality step, but it is also the earliest point to detect **data poisoning** and **tampering** (Module 3.3). Useful checks include:
- **Schema, type and range** validation, so malformed or out-of-range values are rejected.
- **Statistical profiling** of features and labels against a trusted baseline, flagging distribution shifts between batches.
- **Duplicate and near-duplicate detection**, which reduces memorisation and catches repeated injected samples.
- **Label consistency checks**, comparing labels with model predictions or with independent annotators, to catch noisy or deliberately flipped labels.
- **Outlier and anomaly detection** on raw inputs and on embeddings, to spot unusual clusters.
- **Sensitive data scanning**, to stop personal data, secrets or restricted content entering training sets.
- **Source integrity checks**, verifying hashes and signatures against custody records.

### Transformation and reproducibility
Every transformation should be performed by **version-controlled code**, in a **reproducible pipeline**, producing a **versioned dataset** with a content hash. Reproducibility matters for security (you can rebuild a clean dataset after an incident), compliance (you can show exactly what data trained a model) and quality (you can explain changes in model behaviour).

Keep training, validation and test sets **strictly separated** to avoid leakage that inflates evaluation results, and keep a **held-out, access-controlled test set** for security and fairness evaluations.

### Retention, archiving and deletion
Retention periods should be defined for raw data, curated datasets, labels, embeddings, synthetic data, training run artefacts and models, balancing reproducibility and audit needs against minimisation and storage limitation. Archives must keep their classification and access controls; old training snapshots are attractive targets because they are often forgotten.

Deletion must be **propagated** using lineage: from source records to dataset versions, retrieval indexes, models (retrain or unlearn according to policy), caches, backups (expiry) and vendors (deletion with certification). **Cryptographic erasure** (destroying keys) is often the practical way to delete data across large, replicated stores and backups; Module 3.4 covers it with media sanitisation.

blocks.title: Onboard a new dataset for training
items: Register and assess
Record the source, owner, licence and lawful basis. Classify the data and run an SDIA if it contains sensitive data.
Transfer securely
Receive the data over an encrypted channel; record its hash and the custody hand-off.
Validate
Run schema, profiling, duplicate, label and anomaly checks. Quarantine failures and investigate them.
Transform and version
Apply de-identification and cleaning with version-controlled code; produce a hashed dataset version with lineage.
Approve for use
The data owner approves the dataset for the specific purpose (for example, fine-tuning a named model), with access limited to that pipeline.
Set retention
Record the retention period and deletion method for the dataset and any derived artefacts.

blocks.title: Earliest effective control
blocks.md: Questions often ask for the **earliest** or **most effective** point to stop bad data. The answer is usually at **collection and validation**, before data reaches training or an index: source vetting, integrity verification, validation and quarantine. Fixing a model after poisoned data has been trained in is far more expensive.

q.q: A new batch of training data shows a sudden shift in label distribution for one class compared with previous batches. What is the BEST next step?
o: Train on it anyway, since label distributions naturally shift between batches over time
Quarantine the batch and investigate the cause, checking source records for tampering or poisoning
Delete all previous batches and retrain only on the newest data, which best reflects current real-world conditions
Increase the learning rate for the affected class so the model adapts to the new distribution
q.why: Unexpected label shifts can indicate errors or deliberate label manipulation. Validation should quarantine and investigate suspicious data before it reaches training.

quiz.q: Who should approve the use of a dataset to fine-tune a model?
o: The data custodian
The dataset’s data owner
Any data scientist on the project
The model vendor
quiz.why: The data owner is accountable for permitted uses of the data. Custodians operate controls on the owner’s behalf.

quiz.q: A model provider uses customers’ prompts to train its own future models. What is its GDPR role for that processing?
o: Processor
Controller
Data subject
Custodian
quiz.why: Using data for its own purposes means the provider determines purposes and means, so it acts as a controller for that processing.

quiz.q: Which term describes a legal requirement that certain data must remain within a country’s borders?
o: Data residency
Data localisation
Data minimisation
Data stewardship
quiz.why: Localisation is a legal mandate. Residency is where data actually sits, often chosen to satisfy localisation or sovereignty concerns.

quiz.q: Which AI-specific factor is MOST often overlooked when assessing cross-border data transfers?
o: The location of the provider’s head office and the law of its contract
Where inference happens, including failover regions and abuse-monitoring logs
The number of users in each country who will have access to the AI system
The model’s parameter count, which determines which export rules apply
quiz.why: Prompts may be processed or logged in other regions, including during failover, which can create unplanned transfers.

quiz.q: What classification should embeddings generated from Confidential documents normally receive?
o: Public, because embeddings can’t be read by people
Internal, one level below their source documents
Confidential, the same as their source documents
Unclassified until a separate assessment is completed
quiz.why: Derived artefacts inherit their source classification; embeddings can be partly inverted and are used to retrieve the original text.

quiz.q: What is the MAIN purpose of a sensitive data impact assessment for AI?
o: To estimate the dataset’s commercial value before it is licensed to a third party
To assess purpose fit, derivation risks and safeguards before sensitive data is used in AI
To replace the DPIA and other assessments with a single AI-specific review document
To label every file in the dataset manually with its sensitivity and retention period
quiz.why: An SDIA examines whether and how sensitive data can safely be used for an AI purpose, and sets conditions.

quiz.q: Which record shows which models were trained on a particular dataset version?
o: Provenance
Lineage records
A retention schedule
A classification label
quiz.why: Lineage tracks the flow from sources through transformations and dataset versions to training runs and models.

quiz.q: What should provenance for a synthetic dataset include?
o: Nothing; synthetic data is generated rather than collected, so it has no provenance to record
The generator model and version, seed data and its provenance, parameters and validation results
Only the file size, record count and date of generation, which identify each synthetic dataset
Only the name of the team that generated it, which is enough to answer any later questions about it
quiz.why: Synthetic data’s trustworthiness depends on how it was generated and validated, including the source of its seed data.

quiz.q: Which control BEST proves a dataset was not altered between two custodians?
o: A signed letter from each custodian confirming the data is unchanged
Matching cryptographic hashes or signatures recorded at each hand-off
Identical file names, sizes and timestamps at each stage of the transfer
Compressing the dataset into a password-protected archive before transfer
quiz.why: Hashes and signatures provide tamper evidence; recorded at each hand-off, they form the chain of custody.

quiz.q: At which lifecycle stage is poisoned or corrupted data cheapest to stop?
o: After deployment, when monitoring reveals unusual outputs
During collection and validation, before any training begins
During model retirement, when all the training data is archived
During the annual audit of the model’s training pipeline
quiz.why: Catching bad data before it is trained into a model avoids costly retraining and incident response.

quiz.q: Who should be able to edit or delete entries in the chain-of-custody log for a training dataset?
o: The data custodian, who keeps the log accurate as transfers happen
No one: entries are append-only and protected from those they record
Any data scientist who handled the dataset during a training run
The vendor that labelled the data, since it knows what it changed
quiz.why: A custody log is only trustworthy if it is append-only and tamper-evident, protected even from the administrators and custodians whose actions it records. Corrections are added as new entries.

quiz.q: A labelled dataset arrives from a supplier, and its hash doesn’t match the value recorded when it was sent. What should happen FIRST?
o: Recompute the hash on a faster machine and use the new value instead
Quarantine it and investigate the cause before it is used for training
Use it for training, but flag the resulting model for later review
Ask the supplier to resend a hash value that matches the received file
quiz.why: A mismatch means the data changed in transit or at rest, through corruption or tampering. Quarantine stops it reaching training until the cause is known. Replacing the expected hash would defeat the control.

exam.q: A data science team wants to reuse three years of customer call transcripts, collected for quality assurance, to train a sales-recommendation model. What should happen FIRST?
o: Start training, since the data is already held in-house and was lawfully collected from customers
Get the data owner’s approval for the new purpose, backed by a privacy assessment of compatibility and basis
Ask the data custodian to copy the transcripts to the training cluster, with access restricted to the team
Anonymise a sample of the transcripts, check the results, and proceed if no names remain in the sample
exam.why: Reuse for a new purpose needs the owner’s decision and an assessment of compatibility and lawful basis. Being in-house doesn’t make a new purpose lawful.

exam.q: A public-sector client requires that its data never leaves the UK. The AI service’s standard configuration routes requests to the nearest available region worldwide. What is the BEST approach?
o: Accept the routing, since all requests are encrypted in transit and the provider is certified
Restrict processing, logging and failover to UK regions in contract and configuration, and verify it
Tell users to work only during UK business hours, when the nearest available region is in the UK
Store all outputs and logs in the UK only, since stored data is what the residency requirement covers
exam.why: Residency must cover processing, logging and failover, not just storage of outputs, and must be verified. Encryption doesn’t change where data is processed.

exam.q: A RAG pipeline splits labelled documents into chunks, but the chunks lose their sensitivity labels. Users start receiving restricted content in answers. What is the root cause and BEST fix?
o: The model is too large and memorises restricted content, so switch to a smaller model
Labels weren’t carried into chunks; propagate labels to the index and filter retrieval by clearance
Users asked questions outside their role, so retrain them on acceptable use of the assistant
The documents were over-classified, so relabel them at a lower level to match how they are used
exam.why: Without labels on chunks, retrieval can’t enforce access. Propagating labels and filtering retrieval fixes the cause.

exam.q: After a supplier reveals that one of its datasets included scraped content without permission, an organisation must find every affected model. Which capability is MOST important?
o: A data classification policy that labels every dataset by sensitivity
Lineage linking source datasets and versions to training runs and model versions
Encryption at rest for every training dataset and model artefact
Model cards for every model, describing its intended use, training data and known limitations
exam.why: Lineage traces each dataset forward to every model it influenced, enabling targeted retraining or withdrawal.

exam.q: A team proposes replacing sensitive customer data with synthetic data and reclassifying it as Public. What should happen before reclassification?
o: Nothing; synthetic data contains no real people, so it can safely be reclassified as soon as it has been generated
Test for leakage of real records, evaluate fidelity and bias, record provenance, and get the owner’s approval
Delete the original customer data first, so that the synthetic dataset can’t be linked back to it
Publish a sample of the synthetic data internally to see whether anyone recognises real customers
exam.why: Generators can memorise and reproduce real records. Privacy, fidelity and bias must be validated, and the owner must approve any reclassification.

exam.q: A customer’s erasure request is fulfilled in the CRM, but their data remains in a fine-tuning dataset, a vector index and backups. Which practice would have prevented this?
o: Encrypting the CRM and every downstream copy with the same customer-specific key, held centrally
Lineage-driven deletion propagation covering datasets, indexes, models, backups and vendors
Annual privacy training for staff who handle erasure requests and customer records
A written erasure procedure for the CRM team, reviewed by the DPO every year
exam.why: Deletion must follow data downstream. Lineage identifies every copy and derived artefact, so deletion can be propagated and verified.

exam.q: Investigators find that a poisoned dataset reached production. Custody records show it passed through three teams, but its integrity was checked just once, when it first arrived from the supplier. What is the MOST important improvement?
o: Reduce the number of teams, so fewer hand-offs need any records
Hash and verify the data at every hand-off, before each team uses it
Encrypt the dataset in transit between each of the three teams
Ask each team to confirm in writing that it changed nothing
exam.why: Hashing and verifying at every hand-off pinpoints where data changed and stops altered data moving on. Encryption in transit protects data on the wire, not changes made while a team holds it, and written assurances prove nothing.
